text: Around 2,000 years ago, ships sailed from Egypt to India's southern coast, riding the monsoon winds.
They went home loaded with pepper, gems, and cotton cloth.
So much gold that the Roman writer Pliny complained about it.
He grumbled that India drained the empire of 50 million sesterces every single year.
Hoards of Roman coins still turn up in South India today.
17 centuries later, someone in India is going to make exactly the same complaint the other way around.
In the north, newcomers from Central Asia, the Kushans, built an empire,
and their greatest king became a champion of Buddhism.
Remember our question? They came as outsiders, they stayed, and became part of India. Then
around 320 CE a new family united the north, the Gupta's. And what people remember about
the Gupta Age isn't its battles, it's its ideas. In 499, a 23-year-old mathematician
named Ariabot wrote that the earth spins on its own axis. That's about a thousand
years before Copernicus. So the sky turns around the earth every night? No, the
earth turns. The sky stays still. Then why am I not dizzy? I'll explain
tomorrow if the earth is still here.
